claim: A major subpopulation of monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs) contains high levels of dUTP.
source: We report that a major subpopulation of monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs) contains high levels of dUTP, which is incorporated into HIV-1 DNA during reverse transcription (U/A pairs), resulting in pre-integration restriction and post-integration mutagenesis.
evidence: Supported by LC-MS analyses showing dUTP/TTP ratio of ~20 for MDMs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I,J) and enzymatic assays showing undetectable dUTPase activity in MDMs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).

claim: High dUTP levels in MDMs are incorporated into HIV-1 DNA during reverse transcription to form U/A base pairs.
source: We report that a major subpopulation of monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs) contains high levels of dUTP, which is incorporated into HIV-1 DNA during reverse transcription (U/A pairs), resulting in pre-integration restriction and post-integration mutagenesis.
evidence: Supported by Ex-ddPCR showing ~70% of gag amplicons from MDMs contained uracil (Figure 1B) and Ex-Seq showing uniform uracilation across the viral genome (Figure 1D).

claim: Uracilation of HIV-1 DNA results in pre-integration restriction in MDMs.
source: We report that a major subpopulation of monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs) contains high levels of dUTP, which is incorporated into HIV-1 DNA during reverse transcription (U/A pairs), resulting in pre-integration restriction and post-integration mutagenesis.
evidence: Supported by data showing ~99% of uracilated viral DNA is destroyed before integration (Figure 3D) and GFP− MDMs had 50-fold reduction in copy number between early DNA intermediates and proviruses (Figure 3D).

claim: Uracilation of HIV-1 DNA results in post-integration mutagenesis in MDMs.
source: We report that a major subpopulation of monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs) contains high levels of dUTP, which is incorporated into HIV-1 DNA during reverse transcription (U/A pairs), resulting in pre-integration restriction and post-integration mutagenesis.
evidence: Supported by sequencing data showing viral genomic RNA from GFP− MDMs had 1.2% mutation frequency while proviral DNA had <0.007% (Figure 5C).

claim: Less than 1% of uracilated HIV-1 DNA successfully integrates in MDMs.
source: After entering the nucleus, uracilated viral DNA products are degraded by the uracil base excision repair (UBER) machinery with less than 1% of the uracilated DNA successfully integrating.
evidence: Based on comparing early DNA intermediates and proviral DNA levels in GFP− MDMs showing ~99% destruction before integration (Figure 3D).

claim: Uracilated viral DNA products are degraded by the uracil base excision repair (UBER) machinery after entering the nucleus.
source: After entering the nucleus, uracilated viral DNA products are degraded by the uracil base excision repair (UBER) machinery with less than 1% of the uracilated DNA successfully integrating.
evidence: Supported by experiments showing hUNG2 overexpression reduced proviral copies 10-fold and eliminated detectable uracil (Figure 4B,C), and Ugi expression increased uracil content dramatically (Figure 4C).

claim: Uracilated proviral DNA showed few mutations.
source: Although uracilated proviral DNA showed few mutations, the viral genomic RNA was highly mutated, suggesting that errors occur during transcription.
evidence: Sequencing of env region in uracilated viral DNA from GFP− MDMs showed <0.007% mutation frequency (text in Results section).

claim: Viral genomic RNA from uracilated proviruses was highly mutated.
source: Although uracilated proviral DNA showed few mutations, the viral genomic RNA was highly mutated, suggesting that errors occur during transcription.
evidence: Extracellular viral RNA from GFP− MDMs showed 1.2% mutation frequency in env region (Figure 5C).

claim: Mutations in viral genomic RNA from uracilated proviruses occur during transcription.
source: Although uracilated proviral DNA showed few mutations, the viral genomic RNA was highly mutated, suggesting that errors occur during transcription.
evidence: The large difference between proviral DNA mutation frequency (<0.007%) and viral RNA mutation frequency (1.2%) suggests transcriptional errors.

claim: Viral DNA isolated from blood monocytes of drug-suppressed HIV-infected individuals contained abundant uracils.
source: Viral DNA isolated from blood monocytes and alveolar macrophages (but not T cells) of drug-suppressed HIV-infected individuals also contained abundant uracils.
evidence: Ex-ddPCR analysis showed five of six donor monocyte samples contained 20-80% uracil-positive pol amplicons (Figure 7B).

claim: Viral DNA isolated from alveolar macrophages of drug-suppressed HIV-infected individuals contained abundant uracils.
source: Viral DNA isolated from blood monocytes and alveolar macrophages (but not T cells) of drug-suppressed HIV-infected individuals also contained abundant uracils.
evidence: Ex-ALU-gag PCR showed ~40% (monocytes) and 80% (alveolar macrophages) of amplicons were positive for uracils (Figure 7B).

claim: Viral DNA isolated from T cells of drug-suppressed HIV-infected individuals did not contain detectable uracils.
source: Viral DNA isolated from blood monocytes and alveolar macrophages (but not T cells) of drug-suppressed HIV-infected individuals also contained abundant uracils.
evidence: Ex-ddPCR showed no detectable uracil in HIV DNA from resting CD4+ T cells (Figure 7B).

claim: The presence of viral uracils in short-lived monocytes suggests their recent infection through contact with virus producing cells in a tissue reservoir.
source: The presence of viral uracils in short-lived monocytes suggests their recent infection through contact with virus producing cells in a tissue reservoir.
evidence: Based on the short several-day half-life of blood monocytes and the requirement for dUTP incorporation during reverse transcription.

claim: MDMs have a dUTP/TTP ratio of approximately 20.
source: LC-MS analyses of the dUTP and canonical dNTP levels in resting and activated CD4+ T cells and MDMs revealed that the dUTP/TTP ratio was ~20 for MDMs, 1.1 for resting CD4+ T cells, and <0.05 for activated CD4+ T cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I,J) (Gavegnano et al., 2012; Hollenbaugh et al., 2014).
evidence: LC-MS measurements of dNTP pools in MDMs (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I,J).

claim: Resting CD4+ T cells have a dUTP/TTP ratio of approximately 1.1.
source: LC-MS analyses of the dUTP and canonical dNTP levels in resting and activated CD4+ T cells and MDMs revealed that the dUTP/TTP ratio was ~20 for MDMs, 1.1 for resting CD4+ T cells, and <0.05 for activated CD4+ T cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I,J) (Gavegnano et al., 2012; Hollenbaugh et al., 2014).
evidence: LC-MS measurements of dNTP pools in resting CD4+ T cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I,J).

claim: Activated CD4+ T cells have a dUTP/TTP ratio of less than 0.05.
source: LC-MS analyses of the dUTP and canonical dNTP levels in resting and activated CD4+ T cells and MDMs revealed that the dUTP/TTP ratio was ~20 for MDMs, 1.1 for resting CD4+ T cells, and <0.05 for activated CD4+ T cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I,J) (Gavegnano et al., 2012; Hollenbaugh et al., 2014).
evidence: LC-MS measurements of dNTP pools in activated CD4+ T cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I,J).

claim: Reverse transcriptase has a nearly identical Km for dUTP and TTP.
source: Since reverse transcriptase has a nearly identical Km for dUTP and TTP (Kennedy et al., 2011), the high ratio of dUTP/TTP indicates that uracil incorporation is a very frequent event during reverse transcription in the cell cytoplasm, which contains no UBER activity.
evidence: Citation to Kennedy et al., 2011.

claim: The high ratio of dUTP/TTP in MDMs indicates that uracil incorporation is a very frequent event during reverse transcription in the cell cytoplasm.
source: Since reverse transcriptase has a nearly identical Km for dUTP and TTP (Kennedy et al., 2011), the high ratio of dUTP/TTP indicates that uracil incorporation is a very frequent event during reverse transcription in the cell cytoplasm, which contains no UBER activity.
evidence: Based on the dUTP/TTP ratio of ~20 in MDMs and the similar Km values for RT.

claim: The cell cytoplasm contains no UBER activity.
source: Since reverse transcriptase has a nearly identical Km for dUTP and TTP (Kennedy et al., 2011), the high ratio of dUTP/TTP indicates that uracil incorporation is a very frequent event during reverse transcription in the cell cytoplasm, which contains no UBER activity.
evidence: Based on established knowledge that UBER machinery is sequestered in the nucleus.

claim: Approximately 10% of infected MDMs were positive for GFP fluorescence after infection with HIVNL4.3(VSVG) or HIVSF162(CCR5).
source: During HIV infection of MDMs ~10% of the infected MDMs were positive for GFP fluorescence after infection with either replication deficient HIVNL4.3(VSVG) or replication competent HIVSF162(CCR5) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Flow cytometry analysis showing 12-15% GFP positive cells (Figure 3A).

claim: The level of GFP-positive MDMs remained constant from about seven to 30 days after infection.
source: This level of infection based on GFP fluorescence remained constant from about seven to 30 days after infection and did not change when the MOI was varied in the range 0.1–10 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Flow cytometry data over 30-day time period (Figure 3A).

claim: The level of GFP-positive MDMs did not change when the MOI was varied in the range 0.1–10.
source: This level of infection based on GFP fluorescence remained constant from about seven to 30 days after infection and did not change when the MOI was varied in the range 0.1–10 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: MOI variation experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: The copy number of early viral gag-containing DNA products in the GFP− MDM population was about seven-fold lower than the GFP+ population at 1 day post-infection.
source: Droplet digital PCR measurements showed that the copy number of early viral gag-containing DNA products in the GFP− population was about seven-fold lower than the GFP+ population at 1 day post-infection (~2 versus 14 copies/cell, Figure 3B).
evidence: ddPCR measurements of reverse transcription intermediates (Figure 3B).

claim: Viral infection is hindered at the entry and/or early reverse transcription steps in the GFP− MDM population.
source: This result suggested that viral infection was hindered at the entry and/or early reverse transcription steps in the GFP− population.
evidence: Based on the seven-fold lower early viral DNA products in GFP− versus GFP+ MDMs.

claim: The GFP− MDM population contained only 1% of the proviral copies seen in the GFP+ MDMs.
source: Using ALU-gag nested qPCR to measure proviral copies (O'Doherty et al., 2002), we found that the GFP- population contained only 1% of the copies seen in the GFP+ MDMs (Figure 3C).
evidence: ALU-gag nested qPCR measurements (Figure 3C).

claim: A potent pre-integration restriction mechanism is present in the GFP− MDM population.
source: The large decrease in copy number between the early DNA intermediates and the provirus stage suggested that a potent pre-integration restriction mechanism was also present in the GFP− population.
evidence: Based on the 50-fold reduction in copy number between early DNA intermediates and proviruses in GFP− MDMs.

claim: The minor GFP+ MDM population had no detectable proviral uracils.
source: The most striking difference between the two MDM populations was that the minor GFP+ population had no detectable proviral uracils, while ~90% of the proviral copies in the major GFP− fraction contained uracil at day one (Figure 3D).
evidence: Ex-ALU-gag nested qPCR showing Frac U = 0 for GFP+ MDMs (Figure 3D).

claim: Approximately 90% of the proviral copies in the GFP− MDM fraction contained uracil at day one post-infection.
source: The most striking difference between the two MDM populations was that the minor GFP+ population had no detectable proviral uracils, while ~90% of the proviral copies in the major GFP− fraction contained uracil at day one (Figure 3D).
evidence: Ex-ALU-gag nested qPCR measurements (Figure 3D).

claim: GFP+ MDMs had a 20-fold lower dUTP/TTP ratio compared to GFP− MDMs.
source: The GFP+ MDMs had a 20-fold lower dUTP/TTP ratio, which stemmed in part from a five-fold higher TTP concentration compared to the GFP− MDMs.
evidence: dNTP measurements in sorted GFP+ and GFP− MDM populations.

claim: GFP+ MDMs had a five-fold higher TTP concentration compared to GFP− MDMs.
source: The GFP+ MDMs had a 20-fold lower dUTP/TTP ratio, which stemmed in part from a five-fold higher TTP concentration compared to the GFP− MDMs.
evidence: dNTP measurements in sorted GFP+ and GFP− MDM populations.

claim: GFP+ MDMs produced 100 to 1000 times more p24 than GFP− MDMs.
source: Consistent with their larger proviral copy numbers, the GFP+ MDMs produced 100 to 1000 times more p24 than the GFP− MDMs and the levels were fairly constant over a 30 day period (Figure 3E).
evidence: p24 ELISA measurements (Figure 3E).

claim: p24 levels from GFP+ MDMs were fairly constant over a 30 day period.
source: Consistent with their larger proviral copy numbers, the GFP+ MDMs produced 100 to 1000 times more p24 than the GFP− MDMs and the levels were fairly constant over a 30 day period (Figure 3E).
evidence: p24 ELISA measurements over time (Figure 3E).

claim: GFP− MDMs showed a 10-fold decrease in p24 levels between day seven and 14.
source: In contrast, the GFP− MDMs showed a 10-fold decrease in p24 levels between day seven and 14 (Figure 3E), which coincides with the 20-fold reduction in proviral copy number in the same time period (Figure 3D).
evidence: p24 ELISA measurements (Figure 3E).

claim: The 10-fold decrease in p24 levels in GFP− MDMs between day 7 and 14 coincides with a 20-fold reduction in proviral copy number in the same time period.
source: In contrast, the GFP− MDMs showed a 10-fold decrease in p24 levels between day seven and 14 (Figure 3E), which coincides with the 20-fold reduction in proviral copy number in the same time period (Figure 3D).
evidence: Comparison of p24 levels (Figure 3E) and proviral copy numbers (Figure 3D).

claim: The expression of detectable levels of p24, but not GFP, in the GFP− MDMs suggests that truncated viral RNAs are being expressed that extend through the p24 coding sequence, but not GFP.
source: The expression of detectable levels of p24, but not GFP, in the GFP− MDMs suggests that truncated viral RNAs are being expressed that extend through the p24 coding sequence, but not GFP.
evidence: Based on detection of p24 but absence of GFP in GFP− MDMs.

claim: Viral uracils originate primarily from dUTP incorporation during reverse transcription.
source: The combined results strongly support a mechanism where the viral uracils originate primarily from dUTP incorporation during reverse transcription.
evidence: Based on thymidine supplementation experiments, absence of APOBEC signature mutations, and presence of uracils on both DNA strands.

claim: Reverse transcriptase utilizes dUTP with the same efficiency and fidelity as TTP.
source: Since reverse transcriptase utilizes dUTP with the same efficiency and fidelity as TTP (Kennedy et al., 2011), the uracils must be in the form of coding U/A base pairs.
evidence: Citation to Kennedy et al., 2011.

claim: Viral uracils are in the form of coding U/A base pairs.
source: Since reverse transcriptase utilizes dUTP with the same efficiency and fidelity as TTP (Kennedy et al., 2011), the uracils must be in the form of coding U/A base pairs.
evidence: Based on RT utilizing dUTP with same efficiency and fidelity as TTP.

claim: MDMs express very low levels of A3G and A3A.
source: In Figure 2—figure supplement 1, we present immunoblots showing that MDMs express very low levels of A3G and A3A, which is consistent with previous reports and the absence of tell-tale marks of enzymatic deamination described above (Harris and Liddament, 2004).
evidence: Western blot analysis (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: Uracilation was uniform across the HIV viral genome.
source: Thus, about 60% of the 100 bp reads contained uracil, leading us to conclude that uracilation was uniform across the viral genome.
evidence: Ex-Seq analysis showing uniform Frac U across genome positions (Figure 1D).

claim: Over 4000 discordant pairs (integrated proviruses) were identified per million HIV reads for the Seq sample.
source: Over 4000 discordant pairs were identified per million HIV reads for the Seq sample, which was reduced by about 60% for the Ex-Seq sample (Figure 1E).
evidence: Ex-Seq analysis of discordant read pairs (Figure 1E).

claim: Discordant pairs were reduced by about 60% for the Ex-Seq sample compared to the Seq sample.
source: Over 4000 discordant pairs were identified per million HIV reads for the Seq sample, which was reduced by about 60% for the Ex-Seq sample (Figure 1E).
evidence: Ex-Seq analysis of discordant read pairs (Figure 1E).

claim: The level of uracilation in integrated proviruses is similar to that of total HIV DNA.
source: This level of uracilation is similar to that of the total HIV DNA and supports our previous finding that uracils can persist in proviruses when nuclear hUNG2 expression is low (Weil et al., 2013).
evidence: Comparison of uracilation levels in discordant pairs versus total HIV DNA from Ex-Seq.

claim: Uracils can persist in proviruses when nuclear hUNG2 expression is low.
source: This level of uracilation is similar to that of the total HIV DNA and supports our previous finding that uracils can persist in proviruses when nuclear hUNG2 expression is low (Weil et al., 2013).
evidence: Citation to previous work (Weil et al., 2013) and current data on integrated proviruses.

claim: Ex-Seq data showed that uracils appeared on both strands of the viral cDNA.
source: First, Ex-Seq data showed that the uracils appeared on both strands of the viral cDNA rather than the (-) strand that is exclusively targeted by APOBECs (Yu et al., 2004).
evidence: Ex-Seq analysis showing uracils on both DNA strands.

claim: APOBECs exclusively target the (-) strand of viral cDNA.
source: First, Ex-Seq data showed that the uracils appeared on both strands of the viral cDNA rather than the (-) strand that is exclusively targeted by APOBECs (Yu et al., 2004).
evidence: Citation to Yu et al., 2004.

claim: The mutational spectrum of proviral DNA did not match the signature C/G→T/A hotspots for APOBEC cytosine deamination.
source: Second, the mutational spectrum of proviral DNA did not match the signature C/G→T/A hotspots for APOBEC cytosine deamination as determined using the program Hypermut 2.0 (see sequencing studies below) (Rose and Korber, 2000).
evidence: Analysis using Hypermut 2.0 program.

claim: Monocytes and monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs) expressed high levels of SAMHD1 dNTP triphosphohydrolase to reduce the canonical dNTP pools.
source: Using sensitive and specific in vitro enzymatic assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D) (Weil et al., 2013; Hansen et al., 2014; Seiple et al., 2008), we found that monocytes and monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs) expressed high levels of SAMHD1 dNTP triphosphohydrolase to reduce the canonical dNTP pools (Hansen et al., 2014; Goldstone et al., 2011), undetectable dUTPase activity that allowed dUTP accumulation, and modest expression of the UBER enzymes uracil DNA glycosylase (hUNG) and abasic site endonuclease (APE1) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–H).
evidence: Enzymatic assays for SAMHD1 activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).

claim: Monocytes and MDMs have undetectable dUTPase activity that allows dUTP accumulation.
source: Using sensitive and specific in vitro enzymatic assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D) (Weil et al., 2013; Hansen et al., 2014; Seiple et al., 2008), we found that monocytes and monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs) expressed high levels of SAMHD1 dNTP triphosphohydrolase to reduce the canonical dNTP pools (Hansen et al., 2014; Goldstone et al., 2011), undetectable dUTPase activity that allowed dUTP accumulation, and modest expression of the UBER enzymes uracil DNA glycosylase (hUNG) and abasic site endonuclease (APE1) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–H).
evidence: Enzymatic assays for dUTPase activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).

claim: Monocytes and MDMs have modest expression of the UBER enzymes uracil DNA glycosylase (hUNG) and abasic site endonuclease (APE1).
source: Using sensitive and specific in vitro enzymatic assays (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D) (Weil et al., 2013; Hansen et al., 2014; Seiple et al., 2008), we found that monocytes and monocyte-derived macrophages (MDMs) expressed high levels of SAMHD1 dNTP triphosphohydrolase to reduce the canonical dNTP pools (Hansen et al., 2014; Goldstone et al., 2011), undetectable dUTPase activity that allowed dUTP accumulation, and modest expression of the UBER enzymes uracil DNA glycosylase (hUNG) and abasic site endonuclease (APE1) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–H).
evidence: Enzymatic assays for hUNG and APE1 activities (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G,H).

claim: Resting CD4+ T cells have at least seven-fold greater dUTPase activity than MDMs.
source: Although resting CD4+ T cells also possessed high SAMHD1, hUNG and APE activities, their dUTPase activity was at least seven-fold greater than MDMs.
evidence: Comparison of dUTPase activities between cell types (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).

claim: Uracil incorporation is a very frequent event during reverse transcription in MDMs.
source: Since reverse transcriptase has a nearly identical Km for dUTP and TTP (Kennedy et al., 2011), the high ratio of dUTP/TTP indicates that uracil incorporation is a very frequent event during reverse transcription in the cell cytoplasm, which contains no UBER activity.
evidence: Based on dUTP/TTP ratio of ~20 in MDMs and similar Km values for RT.

claim: Overexpression of Ugi in MDMs increased the copy number of early reverse transcription products and proviral DNA about five-fold compared to control.
source: For the cells that were transfected with the Ugi expression plasmid, the copy number of early reverse transcription (RTI) products and proviral DNA was increased about five-fold compared to transfection with the empty control plasmid (Figure 4B).
evidence: qPCR measurements after Ugi transfection (Figure 4B).

claim: Ugi-expressing MDMs had dramatically increased uracil content in viral DNA.
source: The Ugi-expressing cells had dramatically increased uracil content, consistent with efficient knockdown of hUNG2 activity and a prominent role for hUNG2 in uracil excision (Figure 4C).
evidence: Ex-qPCR measurements after Ugi transfection (Figure 4C).

claim: MDMs transfected with the hUNG2 expression plasmid showed a 10-fold reduction in RTIs and proviral DNA relative to control.
source: In contrast, the cells transfected with the hUNG2 expression plasmid showed a 10-fold reduction in RTIs and proviral DNA relative to control (Figure 4B), and we were unable to detect any uracil in viral DNA using Ex-qPCR (Figure 4C).
evidence: qPCR measurements after hUNG2 transfection (Figure 4B).

claim: No uracil was detected in viral DNA from MDMs overexpressing hUNG2.
source: In contrast, the cells transfected with the hUNG2 expression plasmid showed a 10-fold reduction in RTIs and proviral DNA relative to control (Figure 4B), and we were unable to detect any uracil in viral DNA using Ex-qPCR (Figure 4C).
evidence: Ex-qPCR measurements after hUNG2 transfection (Figure 4C).

claim: The hUNG2 nuclear isoform selectively disappeared between 1 and 7 days post-infection with HIVSF162(vpr+), but not with HIVNL4.3(Δvpr).
source: Infections with HIVSF162(CCR5) and HIVNL4.3(Δvpr) showed that the hUNG2 nuclear isoform (but not the mitochondrial hUNG1 isoform) selectively disappeared between 1 and 7 days post-infection with HIVSF162(vpr+), but not with HIVNL4.3(Δvpr) (Figure 4D) (Eldin et al., 2014).
evidence: Western blot analysis (Figure 4D).

claim: The mitochondrial hUNG1 isoform did not disappear during infection with HIVSF162(vpr+).
source: Infections with HIVSF162(CCR5) and HIVNL4.3(Δvpr) showed that the hUNG2 nuclear isoform (but not the mitochondrial hUNG1 isoform) selectively disappeared between 1 and 7 days post-infection with HIVSF162(vpr+), but not with HIVNL4.3(Δvpr) (Figure 4D) (Eldin et al., 2014).
evidence: Western blot analysis (Figure 4D).

claim: Infection with HIVNL4.3(Δvpr) reduced the overall proviral copies present in the mixed population of GFP+ and GFP− MDMs.
source: As expected, infection with HIVNL4.3(Δvpr) reduced the overall proviral copies present in the mixed population of GFP+ and GFP− MDMs (Figure 4E), which is a non-specific effect that can be attributed to any of the known pro-infective functions of vpr (Eldin et al., 2014).
evidence: ALU-gag nested qPCR measurements (Figure 4E).

claim: In the absence of vpr, two-fold fewer proviruses contained uracil.
source: In the absence of vpr, two-fold fewer proviruses contained uracil, which is a uracilation-specific effect that can be attributed specifically to vpr-induced depletion of hUNG2 activity in GFP− MDMs (Figure 4F) (Grogan et al., 2011).
evidence: Ex-ALU-gag nested qPCR measurements (Figure 4F).

claim: The EVR copies present in the supernatant of GFP− MDMs at three days post-cytokine stimulation was about 100-fold lower than the GFP+ population.
source: The EVR copies present in the supernatant of GFP− MDMs at three days post-cytokine stimulation was about 100-fold lower than the GFP+ population, independent of cytokine stimulation.
evidence: qRT-PCR measurements of extracellular viral RNA (Figure 5B).

claim: The lower copies of genomic RNA produced from uracilated proviruses in GFP− MDMs is comparable to the reduced proviral copy number in this population.
source: The lower copies of genomic RNA produced from the uracilated proviruses in GFP− MDMs is comparable to the reduced proviral copy number in this population.
evidence: Comparison of EVR copies and proviral copy numbers in GFP− MDMs.

claim: Uracilation does not significantly alter the output of viral RNA genomes when normalized for proviral DNA levels.
source: This result indicates that uracilation does not significantly alter the output of viral RNA genomes when normalized for proviral DNA levels.
evidence: Based on comparable ratios of EVR to proviral DNA in GFP− and GFP+ MDMs.

claim: Inflammatory cytokine IFNγ stimulation reduced the EVR copy number in both MDM populations by almost 10-fold.
source: We also found that inflammatory cytokine IFNγ stimulation reduced the EVR copy number in both MDM populations by almost 10-fold (Figure 5B), which is therefore not correlated with the uracilation phenotype.
evidence: qRT-PCR measurements with IFNγ stimulation (Figure 5B).

claim: The GFP+ MDM population showed no detectable mutations in the V3/V4 variable region of env regardless of cytokine stimulation.
source: Regardless of cytokine stimulation, the GFP+ population showed no detectable mutations in the roughly 12,000 total bases of the V3/V4 variable region of env that were sequenced.
evidence: Limiting dilution clonal sequencing of extracellular viral RNAs (Figure 5C).

claim: The GFP− MDM population showed a 1.2% basal mutation frequency in the V3/V4 variable region of env.
source: In contrast, the GFP− population showed a 1.2% basal mutation frequency, which responded differently to IFNγ and IL-4 stimulation: IFNγ stimulation increased the frequency by two-fold and IL-4 decreased it significantly (Figure 5C).
evidence: Limiting dilution clonal sequencing of extracellular viral RNAs (Figure 5C).

claim: IFNγ stimulation increased the mutation frequency in GFP− MDMs by two-fold.
source: In contrast, the GFP− population showed a 1.2% basal mutation frequency, which responded differently to IFNγ and IL-4 stimulation: IFNγ stimulation increased the frequency by two-fold and IL-4 decreased it significantly (Figure 5C).
evidence: Limiting dilution clonal sequencing with IFNγ stimulation (Figure 5C).

claim: IL-4 stimulation significantly decreased the mutation frequency in GFP− MDMs.
source: In contrast, the GFP− population showed a 1.2% basal mutation frequency, which responded differently to IFNγ and IL-4 stimulation: IFNγ stimulation increased the frequency by two-fold and IL-4 decreased it significantly (Figure 5C).
evidence: Limiting dilution clonal sequencing with IL-4 stimulation (Figure 5C).

claim: The cytokine environment of an in vivo infected macrophage could influence the evolution of uracilated proviruses.
source: These results suggest that the cytokine environment of an in vivo infected macrophage could influence the evolution of uracilated proviruses.
evidence: Based on differential mutation frequencies with IFNγ and IL-4 stimulation.

claim: The LTR region of EVRs produced from GFP− cells was devoid of detectable mutations after sequencing 7392 total bases.
source: In contrast to the mutated env sequences, the LTR region of EVRs produced from the GFP− cells was devoid of detectable mutations after sequencing 7392 total bases (Supplementary file 1), which may reflect selection for expression of transcription competent LTR sequences.
evidence: Sequencing of LTR region (Supplementary file 1).

claim: The absence of mutations in the LTR region may reflect selection for expression of transcription competent LTR sequences.
source: In contrast to the mutated env sequences, the LTR region of EVRs produced from the GFP− cells was devoid of detectable mutations after sequencing 7392 total bases (Supplementary file 1), which may reflect selection for expression of transcription competent LTR sequences.
evidence: Based on absence of mutations in LTR despite mutations in env.

claim: Targeted sequencing of the env amplicon in uracilated viral DNA isolated from GFP− MDMs at day 14 post-infection revealed a <0.007% mutation frequency in the V3/V4 variable region.
source: Targeted sequencing of the env amplicon in uracilated viral DNA isolated from GFP− MDMs at day 14 post-infection in the absence of cytokine stimulation revealed a <0.007% mutation frequency in the V3/V4 variable region, which is significantly lower than the 1.2% frequency in EVRs produced from the same cell culture (most viral DNA is integrated at day fourteen).
evidence: Targeted sequencing of proviral DNA.

claim: The EVR mutations arise from transcriptional errors by RNA polymerase II (RNAP II).
source: This result suggests that the EVR mutations arise from transcriptional errors by RNA polymerase II (RNAP II).
evidence: Based on low mutation frequency in proviral DNA (<0.007%) versus high frequency in EVRs (1.2%).

claim: RNA mutations may derive from encounter of the polymerase with either uracils or repair intermediates resulting from uracil excision.
source: Such mutations may derive from encounter of the polymerase with either uracils or repair intermediates resulting from uracil excision (see Discussion).
evidence: Speculation based on the presence of uracils and UBER activity.

claim: The RNA (+) strand mutations were primarily single base changes mostly comprised of A→G, A→C, and T→C transitions and transversions.
source: The RNA (+) strand mutations were primarily single base changes mostly comprised of A→G, A→C, and T→C transitions and transversions (Figure 5D,E), but also a few short 2–3 nucleotide insertions or deletions.
evidence: Sequencing analysis of EVRs (Figure 5D,E).

claim: A detailed analysis of the sequence dependence of the observed G→A (+) strand mutations indicated that the sequences and frequencies were not consistent with A3G, A3F or A3A deaminase activity on the viral (-) strand cDNA.
source: A detailed analysis of the sequence dependence of the observed G→A (+) strand mutations using Hypermut 2.0 (Rose and Korber, 2000) indicated that the sequences and frequencies were not consistent with A3G, A3F or A3A deaminase activity on the viral (-) strand cDNA (Yu et al., 2004).
evidence: Analysis using Hypermut 2.0 program.

claim: Proviral DNA isolated from T cells infected with HIVBAL(CCR5) had a much higher mutation frequency (~1%) than uracilated viral DNA in MDMs (<0.007%).
